sections.label: Overview
sections.purpose: Concise scholarly summary of the figure, name, tradition, and significance.
sections.body:
**Diti** (*diti*) ​— Mother ‌of the ‌Daityas · ​Daughter of ​Dakṣa and wife ​of the ​sage Kaśyapa, ​mother of ‌the Daityas, the ​demon race ​— the ‌counterpart of ​her sister ‌Aditi, who is ​mother of ‌the gods ​— belongs ​to the ​Sanskrit tradition, where ​it is ​catalogued under ‌the domain ​"Mother of Demons". ‌The name ​means "Daughter ‌of Dakṣa ​and wife ‌of the sage ​Kaśyapa, mother ‌of the ​Daityas, the ​demon race — ‌the counterpart ‌of her ‌sister Aditi, ​who is ​mother of the ‌gods."[^1].

**Diti** ​is the ​mother of ‌the anti-gods: ​the Daityas, the ​demonic dynasty ‌whose wars ​with the ‌gods drive half ​the Purāṇic ​mythology. Daughter ​of Dakṣa, ​wife of ‌the sage Kaśyapa, ‌twin in ​name of ‌the unfettered ​Aditi, she ​mothers the bound ‌ones — ‌the race ‌of Hiraṇyākṣa ‌and Hiraṇyakaśipu, whose ​boons made ‌them nearly ​invincible.[^2]

PuniCodex ​restores the ​name as **Diti** ‌and serves ​its temple ​at [its ​temple](https://punicodex.com/diti/). The restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent form ​— a ​description computed ​from the ‌displayed form itself. ​The plain ‌ASCII form ​*diti* survives ‌as a ​modern convenience imposed ‌by the ‌early domain-name ​system; the ​restoration, not the ​fallback, is ​the form ‌the project ‌defends as ​philologically complete[^3].

sections.label: The Name
sections.purpose: Etymology, ASCII constraint, Unicode restoration, name variations, tier classification.
sections.body:
The ​name is ‌attested ‌in ​Devanagari as ​**दिति**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Daughter ‌of ​Dakṣa and ​wife ‌of ​the sage ‌Kaśyapa, ​mother ‌of the ​Daityas, ​the demon ​race ​— ​the counterpart ‌of ​her ‌sister Aditi, ​who ‌is ​mother of ‌the ​gods."[^1].

‌The ASCII ​form ​*diti* ‌survives only ‌because ‌the early ​domain-name ​system ‌could not ​carry ​diacritics; ‌it is ​a ​technological ‌compromise, not ​an ‌ancient ​spelling. The ​Unicode ​restoration ​**Diti** recovers ‌the ‌full ​diacritic detail ‌of ​the scholarly ​transliteration ‌directly ‌in the ‌address ‌bar. ​The restoration ‌aSCII-equivalent ​form ​— a ​description ‌computed ​from the ​displayed ​form ‌itself.

The ​letter-by-letter ​transformation runs:

- ​**d** ‌→ ​**D** — ‌Same, ​capitalized
- ‌**i** → ​**i** ‌— ‌Same
- **t** ​→ ​**t** ​— Same
- ​**i** ‌→ ‌**i** — ​Same

sections.label: Pronunciation
sections.purpose: IPA reconstruction, phoneme breakdown, approximation, kin forms.
sections.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of ‌the ​name is ​**/ˈdiːti/** ​— ​Sanskrit (IAST: ​Diti).[^1]

‌Phoneme ​by phoneme:

- ​**Di-** ‌— ​Long ī ‌as ​in ‌“see”; the ​name ​is ​a-diti with ​the ​negation ‌removed.
- **-ti** ​— ‌The ​feminine abstract ‌ending; ​the ‌name means ​“the ‌bound ​one”.
- **** ​— ‌The ‌sister of ‌Aditi ​— ​boundless — ‌and ​mother ​of the ‌anti-gods.

​For ​the modern ‌speaker, ​the closest ‌approximation ​is: ​“DEE-tee”

Kindred ​and ​historical ‌forms of ‌the ​name:

- ‌**Sister** — ​Aditi ​— ‌the unfettered; ‌Diti ‌is ‌her bound ​twin ‌in ​name
- **Sons** ​— ​the ‌Daityas — ​Hiraṇyākṣa, ​Hiraṇyakaśipu, ​and the ‌rest

​The ​name is ​a ‌mirror ​of her ‌sister’s: ​where ‌Aditi is ​“un-bound”, ‌Diti ‌is the ​“bound” ​— ​and her ​sons ‌are ‌the gods’ ​enemies.

sections.body:
**Diti** ​is the ‌mother ‌of ​the anti-gods: ​the ​Daityas, the ​demonic ​dynasty ‌whose wars ​with ​the gods ‌drive ​half the ‌Purāṇic ​mythology. ‌Daughter of ​Dakṣa, ​wife of ​the ​sage ​Kaśyapa, twin ‌in ​name of ‌the ​unfettered ‌Aditi, she ​mothers ‌the bound ​ones ‌— ​the race ​of ‌Hiraṇyākṣa and ‌Hiraṇyakaśipu, ‌whose boons ​made ​them ‌nearly invincible.[^1]

### ​Mother ​of the ‌Daityas

​Her ​sons are ‌the ​Daityas — ‌the ​anti-gods ​whose wars ​with ​the devas ‌fill ‌the ​Purāṇas.

### Sister ‌of ​Aditi

Daughter ​of ‌Dakṣa, sister ‌of ‌the ‌unfettered Aditi ​— ‌her name ​is ​Aditi’s ​negated.

### The ‌Vajra ​Wound

Indra’s ​thunderbolt ​shattered ‌her womb ​mid-pregnancy; ​the fragments ​became ‌the ​Maruts.

### Boons ‌of ​Her Sons

‌Hiraṇyakaśipu’s ​boon made ‌him ‌deathless ​by day ​or ​night, indoors ​or ‌out ‌— until ​Narasiṃha.

sections.label: Symbols
sections.body:
The ​iconography ‌associated ‌with ​Diti ​concentrates ​in ​a ​small ‌set of ​recurring ​attributes, ‌each ​a ‌compressed ​statement ‌about ​the ​name:[^1]

- ​**Mother ​of ​the ‌Daityas** ​— ‌Her ​sons ‌are the ​Daityas ‌— ​the ‌anti-gods ​whose ​wars ‌with ‌the ‌devas ​fill ​the ‌Purāṇas.
- ​**Sister ​of ‌Aditi** ​— ​Daughter ‌of Dakṣa, ​sister ‌of ​the ​unfettered ​Aditi ​— ‌her ‌name ​is ‌Aditi’s ​negated.
- ​**The ‌Vajra ‌Wound** ‌— ‌Indra’s ​thunderbolt ‌shattered her ​womb ​mid-pregnancy; ​the ‌fragments ​became ​the ​Maruts.
- ‌**Boons ​of ​Her ​Sons** ‌— ​Hiraṇyakaśipu’s ‌boon ​made ‌him ​deathless by ‌day ‌or ​night, ​indoors ​or ​out ‌— ‌until ​Narasiṃha.

sections.label: Mythology
sections.purpose: Core myths, primary narratives, and textual evidence.
sections.body:
Diti’s mythology ​is her maternity: everything ‌the Daityas do, ‌she enables — ​and one thing she ​undoes, in the ​Maruts episode, where ​Indra’s violence against her ​pregnant body produces ‌the storm-gods from ​the womb’s fragments. She ​is the anti-mother ‌of the anti-gods, ​the bound one whose ‌children strain against ​every bond except ‌hers.[^1]

### The Maruts from ​the Broken Womb ​(Ṛgveda 1.99)

The ​oldest Diti-story has Indra ​hurl the vajra ​into her womb, ‌shattering a hundred sons ​in embryo; the ‌fragments become the ​Maruts, the storm-gods who ‌yet serve Indra. ​Diti’s grief and ‌the storm-gods’ loyalty are ​the hymn’s tension: ‌the anti-mother’s broken ​children, adopted by her ​enemy.[^2]

### The Boon ‌of Hiraṇyakaśipu (Purāṇic ‌Cycle)

Her son Hiraṇyakaśipu, ‌devastated by his ​brother Hiraṇyākṣa’s death ​at Varāha’s tusk, won ‌from Brahmā the ​boon that he ​could not die by ‌day or night, ​indoors or out, ​by man or beast, ‌on earth or ​sky. The boon made ‌him lord of ​the three worlds ​— until Narasiṃha, the ​man-lion at dusk ​on a threshold, ‌ended him. Diti’s line ‌is the engine ​of the avatāra ‌cycle.

### The Grandson Who ​Worshipped the Enemy ​(Prahlāda Cycle)

Prahlāda, ‌son of Hiraṇyakaśipu and ‌thus Diti’s grandson, ‌loved Vishnu from ‌the womb — the ​devotee born in ‌the anti-god’s house. ​The Purāṇas make his ​devotion the theology ​of bhakti itself: ‌the bound dynasty’s finest ​fruit was the ​boy who could ​not be burned, poisoned, ‌or thrown, for ​his god held ​him.

### Daughter of Dakṣa, ​Wife of Kaśyapa ‌(Genealogical Frame)

The ​Purāṇic theogonies make Diti ‌one of Dakṣa’s ​thirteen daughters given ‌to Kaśyapa: Aditi mothers ​the Ādityas, Diti ‌the Daityas, Danu ‌the Dānavas, and the ​rest of creation’s ​factions follow the ​wives. The marriage-bed of ​Kaśyapa is, in ‌the genealogists’ scheme, ‌the factory of the ​cosmos’s parties.

sections.label: Vedic References
sections.body:
The Vedas, the oldest stratum of Sanskrit scripture, contain hymns and litanies that name or allude to Diti. Ṛgvedic, Yajurvedic, and Atharvavedic passages establish the figure's early association with mother of demons.

The IAST restoration Diti marks the scholarly transliteration of those Vedic passages.[^1]
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Upaniṣads
sections.body:
The Upaniṣads shift the focus from ritual to metaphysics, reinterpreting divine names as symbols of ultimate reality. Diti appears or is implied in passages that map the pantheon onto the self and the cosmos.

The restored form Diti carries the diacritic precision of Sanskrit scholarship.[^1]
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Purāṇas
sections.body:
The Purāṇas narrate the myths, genealogies, and iconographies of Diti in encyclopedic Sanskrit compendia. Texts such as the Viṣṇu Purāṇa, Śiva Purāṇa, and Devībhāgavata Purāṇa shape the devotional identity of the figure.

The IAST form Diti is the scholarly anchor across these compendia.[^1]
sections.editorNotes: Synthesized from canonical sources by PuniCodex Team.

sections.label: Mantras & Stotras
sections.body:
Mantras and stotras addressed to Diti encode the name in ritual sound, often accompanied by visualizations and offerings. The syllabic structure of Sanskrit lends itself to sonic veneration.

The restored spelling Diti preserves the precise phonetic value used in recitation and scholarly citation.[^1]
